newsitem.title: CROATIA: Returning Serbs evicted from Croatia home - UN.
newsitem.headline: Returning Serbs evicted from Croatia home - UN.

text.p: The first Serb refugee family to return to their home town in a reconquered region of Croatia has been swiftly evicted despite Zagreb's pledge to resettle minorities who fled from war, U.N. sources said on Wednesday.

The reported incident in the former rebel Serb enclave of Krajina recaptured in a 1995 Croatian army blitz over truce lines occurred a day after a U.N.-Croatian accord on a "two-way return" of Croat and Serb war refugees.

U.N. relief sources who asked not to be named said a Serb family returned to the town of Kistanje on Saturday and moved into the home they had fled in 1995, only to be kicked out hours later after it was surrounded by angry Croats.

"The family told us they had to leave under duress. The (local) housing commission presented them with a document to sign saying they were leaving willingly but they refused to sign it," a United Nations official told Reuters.
She said the family was staying temporarily in nearby Knin, the largest town in the old Krajina located inland from Croatia's central Adriatic seaboard.
Croatian state officials were unavailable for comment on the case.
Kistanje was razed by vengeful Croat nationalists in the aftermath of the Krajina's fall to government troops that ended a four-year separatist revolt in the Serb-majority region.

The Croatian government has since rebuilt Kistanje to resettle Croat emigrants from Serbia there, although the town once had an overwhelming Serb majority and might draw back its former residents under the "two-way return" plan.

"Croatia has been resettling Croats from Janjevo in (the Serbian province of) Kosovo there but these Croats are also visiting uninhabited Serb homes to move in (without authorisation) or to loot them," she said.

Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, and Croatian President Franjo Tudjman agreed last week to create a working group dedicated to returning both Croat and minority Serb victims of a 1991-95 war to their original homes in Croatia.

This would mean Croats repopulating Croatia's one remaining Serb enclave, Eastern Slavonia, now under U.N. administration but due to be reintegrated with the rest of the country after elections next month.
It would also entail Serb refugees, many now in Eastern Slavonia, moving back into formerly embattled western areas including the Krajina that they abandoned when Croatia reconquered it.
Major obstacles to such returns so far have included a shortage of housing and local ethnic animosities.

"The eviction is very upsetting because if Serbs who return to Kistanje get tossed out of homes they own, it means Serb refugees now in Eastern Slavonia will have nowhere to go when the original Croat residents return there. It would be a vicious circle without end," a U.N. humanitarian official said.
The Serb family ejected from the Kistanje house had come from Eastern Slavonia, at the other end of the country.
"We have expressed deep concern to Croatian authorities about the serious situation for would-be Serb returnees in the old Krajina," the U.N. official said.
Ogata said the two-way return plan was meant to ensure "equal access of Serb and Croat people to housing, economic reconstruction, pensions and various compensation mechanisms".
